articles.summary: On a Monday night in September 1964, television viewers watched a little girl counting petals on a flower. Her voice gave way to a man counting down, and then a nuclear blast filled the screen. The ad ran as a paid spot only once , in support of President Lyndon B. Johnson’s reelection campaign. It never mentioned his opponent, republican Barry Goldwater . The ad played on a fear voters already held, that Goldwater might start a nuclear war . Republicans protested loudly, Democrats pulled the spot, and the uproar got it rebroadcast in full on network news. Formally titled ‘Peace, Little Girl,’ this political commercial was produced for President Lyndon B. Johnson’s 1964 campaign against Barry Goldwater. I study how emotional appeals persuade, from how viewers’ moods shape their reactions to political ads to how anxiety drives people to seek out , and sometimes fail to absorb, information about threats. There are hotel beds you enjoy during your stay—and then there are hotel beds you miss post-checkout. I’m talking about the kind of beds that make you question every life choice the moment you get home and realize just how underwhelming your own sheets really are. At The Ritz-Carlton, Lake Tahoe , the bed is firmly in the second category. Think smooth, cool cotton against your skin, pillows stacked just high enough to feel indulgent, and a cloud-like duvet that manages to feel both weightless and cocooning at the same time. According to Braulio Arizmendi, Director of Room Operations at The Ritz-Carlton, Lake Tahoe, that reaction is intentional. “It feels like being wrapped in softness the moment you settle in,” he says. “Supportive, warm, and instantly calming.” Guests often describe the experience as the perfect balance between plushness and structure—indulgent without being overwhelming.
